landing.faq1A: ChessInt (short for Chess Intelligence) is a free web app that analyzes your own Chess.com and Lichess games. It runs engine analysis on your whole history, gives every move a game review, finds the weaknesses you repeat, and writes you a personal AI coaching report.
landing.faq2A: Yes. Engine analysis, the move-by-move game review, weakness detection, and puzzles are free with no game limit. The engine runs in your browser, so there is no analysis queue.
landing.faq3Q: Does ChessInt work with both Chess.com and Lichess?

landing.faq4Q: How is ChessInt different from the Chess.com game review?

landing.faq5Q: Is ChessInt the same as Chessnut?

settings.title: Settings
settings.emailHint: Your account email cannot be changed.

accuracy.short: How close your moves were to the best moves, scored 0–100%. Higher is better — 90%+ is excellent, under 70% means several moves went wrong.
accuracy.long: Accuracy rolls every move of a game into one friendly number. It is built from how much each move changed your chance of winning, not from raw engine points, so it is easy to compare between games.

cpl.short: How much a move 'cost' you, measured in 1/100ths of a pawn. 0 is perfect; under ~20 is fine; big numbers mean a big mistake.
cpl.long: Centipawn Loss is the gap between the move you played and the best available move. Because a pawn is worth 100 centipawns, a CPL of 50 means you gave up about half a pawn of advantage.

acpl.short: Your Centipawn Loss averaged over a whole game (or many games) — a single number for how cleanly you played. Lower is better.
acpl.long: ACPL is the most common way to compare how well two players, or two of your own games, were played. Strong club players often average under 30.

centipawn.short: A unit for measuring advantage: 100 centipawns = the value of one pawn. The engine scores every position this way.

evaluation.short: The engine's score for a position. Positive = you're better, negative = your opponent is. +1.0 ≈ a pawn ahead, +3.0 ≈ a piece ahead.
evaluation.long: The evaluation is the engine's overall judgement of who stands better and by how much, considering material, king safety, activity, and more.

winpct.short: Your estimated chance of winning from a position, based on the engine's evaluation. Easier to read than centipawns.

blunder.short: A serious mistake that badly hurts your position — usually hanging a piece or missing a major threat. ChessInt marks these so you can learn from them.

mistake.short: A clear error that worsens your position — less severe than a blunder, but it still hands your opponent an edge.

inaccuracy.short: A small slip: not losing, but not the best move. A series of these quietly adds up.

brilliant.short: A great, often surprising move — usually a smart sacrifice the engine confirms is best. The hardest classification to earn.

best.short: You played the engine's top choice for that position.

book.short: A known opening move from established theory — solid, but it's memorised theory rather than your own calculation.

miss.short: You had a strong tactic or winning chance available and didn't play it.

opening.short: The first stage of the game (roughly the first 10–15 moves), where you develop your pieces and fight for the centre.

middlegame.short: The main battle after the pieces are developed — plans, attacks, and tactics. Where most games are won or lost.

endgame.short: The final stage, with few pieces left. Technique matters most here: king activity, passed pawns, and known winning methods.

tilt.short: Playing worse because of emotion — frustration after a loss leading to rushed, weaker moves. ChessInt can spot it in your results.

stockfish.short: The free, world-class chess engine ChessInt runs in your browser to analyse your games.

capablanca.title: Play like Capablanca
capablanca.intro: José Raúl Capablanca won by radical simplicity. He avoided opening theory, disliked long calculation, and almost never blundered. His secret was a small set of positional rules, applied consistently — build a position where all your pieces are active and your opponent's are passive, and the tactics appear on their own. Here is that whole system, for improving players.
capablanca.chaptersHeading: Work through it, with interactive boards
capablanca.chaptersIntro: Each phase is a chapter you can step through move by move on a live board.
capablanca.chFiveRules: Five rules, each on a live board.
capablanca.ch4Desc: The whole method in one steppable model game.
capablanca.loopIntro: This is the habit that drives everything. Before every move, in any phase, ask these three questions in order:

q1.q: What did my opponent just threaten?
q1.hint: If the threat is real, deal with it before anything else. Most games are lost by the player who stops asking this.

q2.q: Which of my pieces is the least active?
q2.hint: If a piece is doing nothing — undeveloped, or stuck with no squares — improving it is usually your best move.

q3.q: Are any enemy pieces or pawns on my half of the board?
q3.hint: An intruder in your camp is dangerous. Trade it, chase it back, or blockade it before it settles in.

capablanca.openingIntro: Capablanca didn't memorise openings — he followed five principles and trusted his understanding for the rest.
capablanca.middlegameIntro: The middlegame is where his method shone: keep improving your pieces until the position becomes overwhelming, and let tactics follow.
capablanca.endgameIntro: Endgames are simpler than they look: win a weak pawn and promote one of your own. Five rules do most of the work.

O-1.title: Develop every piece before you attack
O-1.short: Give every piece a job before starting a plan.
O-1.body: An attack launched with half your army still on the back rank fizzles out — and those sleeping pieces can't defend either. Give every piece a job first. A knight on f3 is working; a knight still on g1 is not.

O-2.title: Break pins calmly
O-2.short: Pinned knight? Support it with the other knight on d2/e2, then unpin.
O-2.body: If a bishop pins your knight, don't panic. Develop your other knight to d2 or e2 to add support, then reposition your queen to undo the pin. You lose no time, because the supporting knight was a useful developing move anyway.

O-3.title: Prefer moves that make a threat
O-3.short: A developing move that also threatens something forces your opponent to react.
O-3.body: The best opening moves develop a piece and create a threat on the opponent's side, forcing them to react and lose time. A check or an attack on a piece can be worth it even if it means moving the same piece twice.

O-4.title: Castle early — usually kingside
O-4.short: Get your king safe as soon as you can; an uncastled king is a liability.
O-4.body: Castle as soon as you reasonably can. Kingside is usually safer — the king hides behind untouched pawns. Queenside is sharper (your rook lands on an open file immediately) but the king is more exposed.

O-5.title: Don't move the same piece twice without a reason
O-5.short: Every wasted tempo gives your opponent a free developing move.
O-5.body: Moving a piece a second time delays developing the rest of your army. The only excuse is a concrete threat — a check, a capture, a fork — that forces your opponent to reply.

M-1.title: Make every piece active before you make a plan
M-1.short: Find your most passive piece and improve it before doing anything else.
M-1.body: The single most important middlegame habit. Before any attack or pawn push, improve your most passive piece. Rooks want open files, knights want strong central squares (d5/e5/d4/e4), bishops want open diagonals, and the queen wants an active but safe post.

M-2.title: After every opponent move, ask what it threatens
M-2.short: Answer 'what does this threaten?' before you look for your own plan.
M-2.body: Before hunting for your own idea, ask what your opponent's move just threatened. This single habit prevents most tactical losses — Capablanca went undefeated for eight years largely because he never stopped asking.

M-3.title: Neutralise enemy pieces on your half
M-3.short: Trade, chase back, or blockade any enemy piece that reaches your side.
M-3.body: Any enemy piece that reaches your half of the board is a problem — deal with it immediately. A knight on d3 is far more dangerous than one on d6. Don't let intruders settle in.

M-4.title: Build domination — tactics appear on their own
M-4.short: Don't hunt tactics; make your pieces active and your opponent's passive.
M-4.body: Don't go looking for combinations. Make all your pieces active and force your opponent's pieces to be passive; once they've run out of good squares, the winning tactic appears by itself. You rarely need to calculate more than a couple of moves ahead.

M-5.title: Choose simple plans
M-5.short: Either attack a weak pawn, or make a passed pawn and push it.
M-5.body: When your pieces are active and you need a plan, pick one of two: attack a weak pawn (isolated, doubled, or backward), or create a passed pawn and advance it. Both build lasting pressure with almost no calculation.

E-1.title: Activate your king
E-1.short: Once queens are off, march the king to the centre — it's a fighting piece.
E-1.body: In the endgame the king becomes a strong piece. The moment the queens come off, march it toward the centre (d4/e4/d5/e5). A centralised king is worth about a minor piece; a king hiding in the corner is wasted.

E-2.title: Attack the pawns
E-2.short: Aim your king and rook at the weakest enemy pawn.
E-2.body: You can't checkmate with few pieces, but you can win pawns and promote one of your own. Find the weakest enemy pawn — isolated, doubled, or backward — and direct your king and rook at it.

E-3.title: Rooks belong behind passed pawns
E-3.short: Put your rook behind a passed pawn — yours or theirs.
E-3.body: Behind your own passed pawn, the rook grows stronger as the pawn advances. Behind the opponent's, it restrains the pawn cheaply while your king does other work. A rook in front of a passed pawn is passive and weak.

E-4.title: Don't push pawns without a reason
E-4.short: Every careless pawn move leaves a permanent weakness.
E-4.body: Pawn moves can't be taken back. Advance a pawn only to open a file for your rook, make or support a passed pawn, restrict the enemy king, or escape an attack. Otherwise, leave it alone.

E-5.title: Play on two weaknesses
E-5.short: One target can be defended; two on opposite wings cannot.
E-5.body: Create or find two weak points on opposite sides of the board. Attack one to drag the defender across, then switch to the other — your opponent can't be in two places at once. This is how Capablanca won 'equal' endgames.

capablanca.mindset1Body: Consistent good play with no blunders beats occasional brilliance with occasional disasters. Choose the clear move over the flashy one.
capablanca.mindset2Title: Trade when your pieces are better.
capablanca.mindset2Body: Swapping into an endgame where your pieces are more active is how a positional edge becomes a win. Trading while passive is the mistake.
capablanca.mindset3Body: When there's nothing better, improve your least-active piece by one square and ask again next move. Quiet pressure makes opponents crack.
capablanca.mindset4Body: The question that prevents the loss is the one you actually ask. Make it automatic.
capablanca.gameHeading: A complete game: Capablanca vs. Bernstein, 1914
capablanca.gameIntro: Every rule above appears in this one 36-move masterpiece — develop everything, plant a knight on an outpost, break through only when dominant, then convert with king and passed pawn.

gameMoves.note: An open game — Capablanca was comfortable in any structure.
Both sides develop a knight toward the centre first (O-1).
The Ruy López. Black challenges the bishop straight away.
Everyone keeps developing — nobody wastes a move (O-5).
Capablanca castles as early as he can (O-4).
The rook takes the e-file — every piece gets a job (O-1).
A knight lands on an outpost it can never be kicked off (M-1).
A break that works only because every white piece was already ideal (M-4).
In the endgame the rook invades the 7th rank (E-2).
The king marches to the centre to escort the passed pawn (E-1).
The passed pawn rolls, rook behind it the whole way (E-3). Black resigns.

capablanca.faq1A: José Raúl Capablanca (1888–1942) was the third World Chess Champion and is widely regarded as the greatest natural talent in the game's history. He was famous for winning 'equal' positions through pure technique — Magnus Carlsen has named him a major inspiration.
capablanca.faq2Q: Do I need to memorise openings to play this way?
capablanca.faq2A: No. Capablanca deliberately avoided opening theory. He played natural developing moves and trusted a small set of positional rules. This system is about principles you apply every move, not lines you memorise.
capablanca.faq3Q: How does this help me stop blundering?
capablanca.faq3A: The core habit is asking 'what did my opponent just threaten?' before every move. Most losses aren't failures of calculation — they're moments of inattention where a threat was missed. Making that question automatic prevents the majority of tactical losses.
capablanca.faq4A: Yes — it's arguably the best system for beginners, because it replaces guesswork with a clear procedure: deal with threats, activate your worst piece, keep intruders out, and choose a simple plan.
capablanca.closingTitle: See these rules in your own games.
capablanca.closingBody: ChessInt reviews every game you play and shows exactly where a threat was missed or a piece sat idle — the Capablanca rules, applied to you.
capablanca.opChIntro: Capablanca never memorised opening theory. He followed five simple principles — develop everything, keep your king safe, and never waste a move. Step through each on the board below.
capablanca.mgChIntro: This is where Capablanca's method shone: keep improving your pieces until the position is overwhelming, and let tactics appear on their own. Work through the ideas below.
capablanca.egChIntro: Endgames are simpler than they look: win a weak pawn and promote one of your own. These five rules do most of the work — step through the key techniques on the board.
capablanca.openingChecklistTitle: Opening checklist — ask before each move
openingChecklist: Have I developed a new piece? (Prefer developing over pawn moves.)
Am I moving the same piece a second time? If so — is the reason a concrete threat?
Does my opponent have an immediate threat I need to address?
Am I ready to castle? If yes — castle now.
After castling: which is my least active piece?
capablanca.middlegameChecklistTitle: Middlegame decision tree — work through it in order
middlegameChecklist: Is there a concrete threat? If yes — address it first.
Is any piece passive? If yes — improve it before anything else.
Any opponent pieces on your half? If yes — neutralise them.
Can you attack a weak pawn, or create and advance a passed pawn?
If none of the above — improve your best-placed piece and repeat next move.
endgameChecklist: Has my king moved toward the centre yet? (Priority one.)
Which is the weakest pawn on the board? Is my king heading there?
Is my rook behind my passed pawn (or behind the opponent's)?
Have I avoided pawn moves without a clear reason?
Am I pressing two weaknesses — or only one?
capablanca.gameChTitle: A complete game, move by move
capablanca.gameChIntro: Here is the whole method in one short game — an illustrative model game (not a specific historical one), chosen so every move is either developing a piece or improving one. Step through it and watch a quiet position turn into a strong one, with no tactics forced and nothing left on the back rank.
capablanca.gameChNotice1: Every piece got a job first (O-1) — knights and bishops out before any plan.
capablanca.gameChNotice2: The king was tucked away early (O-4) — castling before the position opened.
capablanca.gameChNotice3: The worst piece was improved (M-1) — the d2-knight rerouted f1–g3, aiming at f5, instead of sitting passively.
capablanca.gameChNotice4: The payoff came last — only once every piece was active did White strike in the centre with d4. Patience, then the break.
capablanca.gameEyebrow: The Capablanca method · A complete game

O-1.start: A London System — develop every piece before starting anything.
O-1.0: Stake a claim in the centre.
O-1.4: Open a path for the bishop.
O-1.6: Every minor piece gets a job before any attack.
O-1.8: Nbd2, not Nc3 — it keeps the c-pawn free and guards f3.

O-2.start: Handling a pin calmly — no panic, no wasted time.
O-2.5: Black pins the f3-knight against the queen.
O-2.6: Bring up the other knight first (O-2).
O-2.8: …then Be2 breaks the pin. Both moves developed a piece — no tempo lost.

O-3.start: A developing move that also makes a threat.
O-3.4: The Ruy López: Bb5 develops AND pressures the knight defending e5 (O-3).
O-3.6: Keep the pressure — every move still develops.

O-4.start: Castle as early as you reasonably can.
O-4.4: The Italian — pieces flow out naturally.
O-4.6: Castle now (O-4): the king is safe and the rook is connected.

O-5.start: Don't move the same piece twice — spend every move developing a new one.
O-5.8: Castled and nearly fully developed — no move wasted moving a piece twice (O-5).

M-1.start: The knight on d5 is a permanent outpost — no black pawn can ever chase it off. That is a maximally active piece (M-1).

M-2.start: Before your own plan, ask what your opponent just threatened (M-2).
M-2.6: White threatens Nxf7 — a real threat that must be met at once.
M-2.7: d5! Identify the threat and answer it before doing anything else.
M-2.9: …and only now continue with your own plan, hitting the bishop.

M-3.start: Black's knight has crashed into d3, deep in White's camp — it even checks the king. Deal with an intruder at once (M-3).
M-3.0: cxd3 — the intruder is eliminated immediately. Don't let enemy pieces settle on your half.

M-5.start: A protected passed c-pawn (defended by b4), with no black pawn able to stop it — a simple, powerful plan (M-5).
M-5.0: c6! It rolls forward and Black's pieces must drop everything to watch it.
M-5.2: c7 — one step from a new queen. The passed pawn has tied Black down completely.

E-1.start: Queens are off — the king becomes a fighting piece. March it to the centre (E-1).
E-1.2: The king is centralised and active, worth about a minor piece here.

E-2.start: Black's d4-pawn is isolated and weak — the primary endgame target (E-2).
E-2.0: Rxd4 — win the weak pawn. Every pawn you collect is a step toward a new queen.

E-3.start: The rook sits BEHIND its passed pawn (E-3) — it will grow stronger with every push.
E-3.0: b4 — the pawn advances, the rook still behind it.
E-3.4: The rook-and-pawn battery is almost impossible to stop.

E-5.start: Black has weak pawns on both wings (a7 and h7). One can be defended — two cannot (E-5).
E-5.0: Attack the a-pawn — Black must rush to defend it.
E-5.2: Switch wings! Now the h-pawn is hanging. The king can't guard both.
E-5.4: Back again — shuttling between two weaknesses until one falls.

game.start: A quiet model game in Capablanca's style — every move develops or improves a piece.
game.4: The Italian — pieces flow out naturally.
game.8: Open the last bishop and support e4.
game.12: The rook takes the e-file, freeing f1 for the knight.
game.14: Nbd2 — heading for a better square (M-1).
game.18: …to g3, eyeing f5 — a far more active post.
game.20: d4! With every piece improved, White finally takes the centre — the payoff of patient play.

howToPlay.title: How to play chess
howToPlay.intro: If you have never played a single game, you are in the right place. By the end of this page you will know how to set up the board, how every piece moves, and how to win. It really does only take a few minutes.
howToPlay.setupBody: Place the board so that each player has a light square in the bottom-right corner — "white on the right." The pieces line up on the two rows nearest each player. Rooks go in the corners, then knights, then bishops, then the queen and king in the middle. The easy rule for the royals: the queen goes on her own colour (the white queen on a light square, the black queen on a dark square), and the king takes the square beside her.
howToPlay.setupDiagramCaption: The starting position. White moves first.
howToPlay.piecesBody: Each type of piece moves in its own way. In every diagram below, the dots show where that piece could move from the middle of an empty board. A piece (except the knight) cannot jump over others, and it captures by landing on an enemy piece's square.
howToPlay.rookBody: The rook moves in straight lines — any number of squares up, down, left, or right.
howToPlay.rookDiagramCaption: A rook on d4 controls its whole row and column.
howToPlay.bishopBody: The bishop moves diagonally, any number of squares. Each bishop stays on one colour for the entire game.
howToPlay.bishopDiagramCaption: A bishop on d4 slides along both diagonals.
howToPlay.queenBody: The queen is the most powerful piece: she combines the rook and bishop, moving any number of squares in a straight line or diagonally.
howToPlay.queenDiagramCaption: The queen: straight lines and diagonals together.
howToPlay.knightBody: The knight moves in an L-shape: two squares one way, then one square at a right angle. It is the only piece that can jump over other pieces. This is the move beginners find strangest — so take a moment with the diagram.
howToPlay.knightDiagramCaption: A knight on d4 reaches eight squares, all an L away.
howToPlay.kingBody: The king moves one square in any direction. He is the most important piece — if he is trapped, the game is over — so he moves carefully.
howToPlay.kingDiagramCaption: The king: one step at a time, in any direction.
howToPlay.pawnBody: Pawns are unusual. They move straight forward one square (or two squares on their very first move), but they capture diagonally — one square forward-left or forward-right. Pawns never move backward.
howToPlay.pawnDiagramCaption: A pawn on e2 can step to e3 or, on its first move, e4.
howToPlay.checkBody: When a king is under attack, it is in check. You must respond immediately — move the king to safety, block the attack, or capture the attacking piece. If there is no legal way to escape the attack, it is checkmate and the game ends. That is how you win: not by capturing the king, but by leaving it with nowhere to go.
howToPlay.castlingBody: — once per game, if neither the king nor a rook has moved and the squares between them are empty, the king slides two squares toward the rook and the rook hops to the king's other side. It tucks your king into safety. You may have seen it written as <term>O-O</term>.
howToPlay.enPassantBody: — a special pawn capture: if an enemy pawn dashes two squares forward and lands right beside your pawn, you may capture it as if it had only moved one square — but only on the very next turn.
howToPlay.promotionBody: — if one of your pawns reaches the far end of the board, it transforms into any piece you choose (almost always a queen). A humble pawn can become your most powerful piece.
howToPlay.drawBody: Not every game ends in a win. The most common surprise is stalemate: if the player to move has no legal move but is not in check, the game is a draw — even if they have far less material. Games are also drawn by agreement, by repeating the same position three times, or when there are too few pieces left to checkmate.
howToPlay.nextBody: That is the whole rulebook. The fastest way to improve from here is to play, then look back at what happened — which is exactly what ChessInt does for you. Two good next steps:
howToPlay.nextItem1: Learn to read the moves in a game with <link>how to read chess notation</link>.
howToPlay.nextItem2: When a term confuses you, the <link>glossary</link> explains it in one sentence.
howToPlay.faq1A: The rules of chess take about 20 minutes to learn — how the pieces move and how to win. Getting good takes longer, but you can play a full game the same day you learn. This guide covers everything you need to start.
howToPlay.faq2Q: Which colour goes first in chess?
howToPlay.faq2A: White always moves first, then players alternate turns. You must move on your turn — you can never skip.
howToPlay.faq3Q: How do you win at chess?
howToPlay.faq3A: You win by checkmate: attacking the opponent's king so that it cannot escape capture on the next move. The king is never actually captured — the game ends the moment escape is impossible.
howToPlay.faq4Q: What is the easiest piece to learn?
howToPlay.faq4A: The rook moves in straight lines and the bishop moves diagonally — both are simple. The knight, which jumps in an L-shape, is the one most beginners find tricky at first.
howToPlay.closingTitle: Played a few games? See what you can improve.

chessNotation.title: How to read chess notation
chessNotation.intro: Every move in your game review is written in a short code. Once you know the code, you can read any game in the world — and follow exactly what ChessInt is showing you.
chessNotation.squareNameBody: The board is a grid. The columns (called files) are lettered a to h from left to right. The rows (called ranks) are numbered 1 to 8 from White's side. Put a letter and a number together and you have named a square — like e4, the famous centre square.
chessNotation.squareNameDiagramCaption: The pawn is on e4: the e-file, the 4th rank.
chessNotation.pieceLettersBody: The knight is N because K is already taken by the king. Pawns get no letter at all — you just write the square.
chessNotation.ptBxe5: a bishop captures on e5 (x = capture).
chessNotation.ptClosing: Moves come in pairs, numbered by turn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 means White played e4 and Black replied e5, then White played Nf3 and Black replied Nc6. That is all a game score is.
chessNotation.faq1Q: What does Nf3 mean in chess?
chessNotation.faq1A: N is the knight (K is already the king), and f3 is the destination square. So 'Nf3' means 'knight moves to the f3 square'. Pawns have no letter — 'e4' just means a pawn moves to e4.
chessNotation.faq2Q: What does the 'x' mean in chess notation?
chessNotation.faq2A: An 'x' means a capture. 'Bxe5' means a bishop captures the piece on e5. For pawn captures you write the starting file, like 'exd5' (the e-pawn captures on d5).
chessNotation.faq3Q: What do O-O and O-O-O mean?
chessNotation.faq3A: O-O is kingside castling (the short one) and O-O-O is queenside castling (the long one). A '+' after a move means check, and '#' means checkmate.
chessNotation.closingBody: New to the game itself? Start with <link1>how to play chess</link1>. Confused by a term? See the <link2>glossary</link2>.

improveMiddlegame.title: How to improve your middlegame
improveMiddlegame.intro: The middlegame is where most games are decided — and where most rating is lost. The good news: you don't need to memorise anything. You need a repeatable way of thinking and a habit of fixing the same leaks. Here is a plan you can actually follow.
improveMiddlegame.h1: 1. Always have a plan (read the pawns)
improveMiddlegame.body1: Aimless moves are the most common middlegame mistake. Before you look for a move, ask what the position wants. The pawn structure usually tells you: open files belong to your rooks, a hole in your opponent's camp wants a knight, a pawn majority on one side wants to advance. A modest plan followed consistently beats brilliant moves chosen at random.
improveMiddlegame.body2: When you don't know what to do, find your least active piece and make it better. A bishop staring at its own pawns, a rook doing nothing on its starting square — fix that. Strong players are relentless about getting every piece working.
improveMiddlegame.body3: This one habit is worth more rating than any opening line. Before you commit, ask: "If I play this, what can my opponent do to me?" Scan their checks, captures, and threats. A blunder — hanging a piece, missing a fork — undoes thirty good moves in one. Slowing down for a five-second safety check is the highest-return change most players can make.
improveMiddlegame.h4: 4. Train the patterns you keep missing
improveMiddlegame.body4: Middlegame tactics — forks, pins, skewers, discovered attacks — are pattern recognition. You get them by seeing them over and over. A few tactics puzzles a day, every day, beats a long session once a week. The most efficient puzzles are the ones drawn from positions you actually got wrong, because those target your real gaps.
improveMiddlegame.h5: 5. Use your own games as the syllabus
improveMiddlegame.body5: Generic advice only goes so far. Your games tell you exactly which of the above to prioritise. In ChessInt, open a game's review and look at the <term>middlegame</term> grade and the moves marked as mistakes — then check your <link>recurring weaknesses</link> to see the pattern across many games. If "missed fork" keeps appearing, you know what to drill this week.
improveMiddlegame.routineBody: 10 minutes of tactics daily · review every game you lose, focusing on the first move ChessInt marks as a mistake · pick one recurring weakness and make beating it your goal for the week.
improveMiddlegame.faq1Q: Why is the middlegame so hard?
improveMiddlegame.faq1A: The opening has known theory and the endgame has known techniques, but the middlegame has the most possibilities and the fewest rules to lean on. That is exactly why a clear thinking routine — plan, candidate moves, blunder-check — helps so much.
improveMiddlegame.faq2Q: How do I stop blundering in the middlegame?
improveMiddlegame.faq2A: Before every move, do a quick safety check: 'If I play this, what does my opponent attack?' Look for their checks, captures, and threats first. Most middlegame points are lost to one-move oversights, not deep strategy.
improveMiddlegame.faq3Q: What should I study to improve my middlegame?
improveMiddlegame.faq3A: Daily tactics (pattern recognition), a little on common pawn structures, and — most useful of all — reviewing your own middlegames to find the mistakes you repeat.
improveMiddlegame.nextBody: Next, the most trainable phase of all: <link>how to improve your endgame →</link>

improveEndgame.title: How to improve your endgame
improveEndgame.intro: If your <term>endgame</term> needs work, you are in luck: it is the most trainable part of chess. Unlike the middlegame, there are only a handful of positions to learn, and they repeat for the rest of your chess life. A few hours here can be worth more than months of opening study.
improveEndgame.body1: The single most important endgame idea. With the queens off the board, the king is no longer in danger — it is a strong piece. March it toward the centre and toward the pawns. In most endgames, the player whose king joins the fight first wins.
improveEndgame.body2Intro: You should be able to deliver these in your sleep, with no thinking:
improveEndgame.kqBody: — push the enemy king to the edge with your queen, then bring your king up to deliver mate. (Careful not to stalemate!)
improveEndgame.krBody: — the "staircase": use king and rook together to force the lone king back rank by rank.
improveEndgame.body2Closing: Failing to convert these is one of the most painful ways to drop a point — and it is completely avoidable with a little drilling.
improveEndgame.h3: 3. Passed pawns and the rule of the square
improveEndgame.body3: A passed pawn — one with no enemy pawns able to stop it — is gold in the endgame. To check if a lone king can catch a runner without help, use the rule of the square: imagine a square whose side is the distance from the pawn to its promotion rank. If the defending king can step into that square, it catches the pawn; if not, the pawn queens. "Passed pawns must be pushed."
improveEndgame.h4: 4. King and pawn vs king: the opposition
improveEndgame.body4: The most important pawn endgame. When the two kings face each other with one square between them, the player not having to move holds the opposition and controls the key squares. Mastering the opposition decides whether a single extra pawn is a win or a draw — and it underlies countless real games.
improveEndgame.h5: 5. Drill, then apply it to your games
improveEndgame.body5: Endgames stick through repetition. Practise the positions above until they feel automatic, then let your own games point you to what matters most. In ChessInt, your game review gives each game an <term>endgame</term> grade and your <link>endgame drills</link> target the exact technique you fumbled. If your endgame grade is low while your opening is strong, this is the cheapest rating you will ever buy.
improveEndgame.routineBody: drill K+Q vs K and K+R vs K until automatic · learn the opposition in king-and-pawn endings · remember "active king, push passed pawns." That covers most of what beginners lose in the endgame.
improveEndgame.faq1A: The endgame is the most trainable phase: there are only a few positions to learn, they come up again and again, and knowing them turns drawn games into wins and lost games into draws. It is the best return on study time for most players.
improveEndgame.faq2Q: What endgames should a beginner learn first?
improveEndgame.faq2A: In order: how to checkmate with king and queen, then king and rook, then king-and-pawn versus king (the 'opposition'). Those three alone decide a huge share of games.
improveEndgame.faq3Q: What is the most important endgame principle?
improveEndgame.faq3A: Activate your king. In the middlegame the king hides; in the endgame it becomes a fighting piece and should march toward the action. An active king is often worth a pawn.
improveEndgame.seeAlsoBody: See also: <link>how to improve your middlegame</link>.
